metadata.title: Analysis of Factors Effecting PISA 2015 Mathematics Literacy via

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 Turkey data for 15-year-old students, with a sampling frame described as 187 schools selected from 61 provinces and 5895 students initially sampled, then an analytic subset of 4422 students is used. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), nor does it name any weight variables from the PISA database. Because the models are implemented in Weka/Matlab/SPSS Modeler and the paper does not discuss complex survey design adjustments, the analysis appears to be conducted without explicit weight-based population representativeness. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA student sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) when estimating uncertainty, and should consider whether the ML evaluation should be adapted to the clustered sampling structure (students within schools).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is derived from PISA mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) by averaging them and then mapping the averaged score into three proficiency categories. However, the paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for questionnaire predictors or for the PV-derived outcome (e.g., whether cases with missing predictor responses were excluded, imputed, or otherwise handled). Given that PISA datasets typically contain some missingness in background items, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect model estimates if missingness is non-random.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 Turkey computer-based assessment data for 15-year-old students from randomly selected schools (187 schools across 61 provinces). The analytic dataset contains 4422 students who participated in the PISA 2015 test and for whom the authors constructed the dependent variable from averaged PV1MATH–PV10MATH and included 25 predictor variables from student questionnaires and scales. The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., missing questionnaire items, outlier removal, or specific completion thresholds), so the filtering beyond the stated analytic sample size is not fully documented.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Mathematics literacy (Turkey; PV1MATH–PV10MATH averaged; proficiency recoded to low/medium/high)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — Correct classification rate: 81.2%, Misclassification rate: 18.8%; Correlation: 0.676193; RMSE: 0.3217; MAE: 0.2064; RAE: 0.5756; RRSE: 0.7377. MLPANN — Correct classification rate: 86.7%, Correlation: 0.638909; RMSE: 0.3927; MAE: 0.2449; RAE: 0.6831; RRSE: 0.9005.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Mathematics literacy (Turkey; PV1MATH–PV10MATH averaged and recoded into low/medium/high) the study leveraged Student anxiety, Turkish success status, Mother education level, Student motivation, and Belief about epistemology to predict Mathematics literacy status, finding that Random Forest achieved lower error (RMSE 0.3217; MAE 0.2064; RRSE 0.7377) and higher correlation (0.676193) than the Multi-layer Perceptron. This indicates that strengthening student anxiety reduction and supporting reading-linked achievement (proxied by Turkish success) alongside family-education supports may improve mathematics proficiency, though the study is predictive and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Turkey data for 15-year-old students (analytic sample N=4422) to predict mathematics literacy status. The dependent variable is constructed by averaging PV1MATH–PV10MATH and then mapping the averaged score into three proficiency categories (low/medium/high) using PISA 2015 mathematics thresholds. Two data-mining models are compared: a Multi-layer Perceptron (MLPANN) and Random Forest (RF). RF shows better error-based performance (RMSE 0.3217 vs 0.3927; MAE 0.2064 vs 0.2449; RRSE 0.7377 vs 0.9005) and higher correlation (0.676193 vs 0.638909), while MLPANN has a higher correct classification rate (86.7% vs 81.2%). The most important predictors for RF include student anxiety, Turkish success status, mother education level, motivation, and epistemological beliefs. The paper does not report a missing-data handling strategy or any use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, limiting uncertainty quantification and generalizability.
